newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-New museum celebrates African American culture.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-New museum celebrates African American culture.

text.p: Twelve-year-old Kristopher Hendricks, dressed in a tan suit and tie, stared at the sculptures of young African boys shackled to the hull of a slave ship and saw himself -- literally.

The centrepiece sculptures in the newly rebuilt Museum of African American History were made from plaster body casts of Hendricks and other Detroit schoolchildren who were chosen because the average age of slaves captured in Africa was 14.
"It makes me proud," Hendricks said of the finished product a few days before the much-expanded museum reopened last week. "I had no idea I would be so realistic-looking."

The recreation of the 70-foot (21 metre) slave ship is the most moving exhibit at the $38.4 million museum, which provides a thought-provoking perspective on the role and contributions of blacks in America.

"When you stand here and see all this, you really get a sense that this isn't just a 'black thing,'" said Hendricks' father, Kevin. "It's clearly a part of all of us, but a part that has never been addressed this way and this clearly."

Listed on the crossbeams of the ship are the names of more than 2,000 such vessels known to have transported African slaves to America. The exhibit also forces visitors to crouch down to see it clearly -- recreating just a tiny bit of the cramped feeling on such vessels.
HOPES TO BE A NATIONAL FORCE

The museum, which has had a low profile since it opened in the 1960s, hopes to become a national force with the opening of its new domed facility set on six acres (2.4 hectares) with a total of 120,000 square feet (11,150 sq metres) of space for exhibitions, classrooms, auditoriums, a library and other facilities.
Exhibits range from a replica of the Birmingham jail house door that slammed shut behind Dr. Martin Luther King to the flight suit worn by black astronaut Mae Jemison.
Carlotta Walls, who as a little girl helped integrate Arkansas schools during the racial fury of the 1950s, has donated the dress she wore on her first day in a white school.

The museum celebrates inventors, musicians, sports figures, business leaders, war heroes and political leaders. It spans history with exhibits detailing the life of blacks over 400 years: tribal feuds in Africa that resulted in the beginnings of European slave trading, slavery in America, the Reconstruction era after the Civil War, the 20th century and strides to equal education, voting rights and civil rights, and modern African American life.

"The biggest surprise that you get when you go through here and see all the pieces put together is the Africa-ness of America today," said museum president Kimberly Camp, a former gallery director at the Smithsonian in Washington. "You don't bring thousands and thousands of people here over 400 years without them having an impact on what's here."

Measuring and detailing that impact is at the core of the museum's mission, Camp said, adding that the museum also hopes to become a top research centre for African American issues. "It is a place to look at ourselves collectively in a fresh way," she said.

It is also a place where white Americans should feel comfortable digesting the deep and distant origins of today's racial rifts. "We have purposely designed 'safe spaces' where people can reflect and contemplate the exhibit and its message," she said.

The new facility, paid for in a bond issue approved by the citizens of Detroit, will have an annual operating budget of $6.2 million, with $1.25 million funded by the city. The Ford Motor Co. recently announced a $1 million donation to the museum.
